newsitem.title: UK: Head of U.S. cloning committee explains ban.
newsitem.headline: Head of U.S. cloning committee explains ban.

text.p: The man who headed a commission that recommended a temporary ban on human cloning explained the group's decision on Thursday, saying it went "to the very nature of what it means to be human".

Writing in the journal Science, Harold Shapiro, chairman of the U.S. National Bioethics Advisory Commission and president of Princeton University, said there were both emotional and scientific considerations in the decision.
The issue of human cloning took on new urgency earlier this year when scientists in Scotland announced they had cloned an adult sheep named Dolly.
Although there was no question that humans would follow anytime soon, the world reacted with horror.
Shapiro's advisory committee of 18 scientists, lawyers and theologians was given 90 days to come up with a report on the implications for cloning people.

"Issues related to human cloning in this novel manner go to the very nature of what it means to be human and to the very heart of what people think of as their families and their individuality," Shapiro wrote.
Last month, President Bill Clinton acted on the group's recommendations and proposed a five-year ban on human cloning.

"We concluded that, at present, the use of this technique to create a child would be a premature experiment that would expose the foetus and the developing child to unacceptable risks," Shapiro wrote.
He said there were also religious issues, with theologians disagreeing.
Congress should pass a law against human cloning, Shapiro's group concluded, but should review it in a few years' time.
